stem: A client's free T4 is below the laboratory reference interval and TSH is elevated. Which thyroid-function pattern does this most strongly suggest?
rationale: The American Thyroid Association states that elevated TSH with low free T4 indicates primary hypothyroidism caused by disease in the thyroid gland. In contrast, central/pituitary hypothyroidism typically has low free T4 with an inappropriately low or non-elevated TSH, and primary hyperthyroidism usually has suppressed TSH with elevated thyroid hormone. A is therefore the best answer.
educational_objective: Recognize elevated TSH with low free T4 as the classic laboratory pattern of primary hypothyroidism.
source_version_date: Current ATA patient/clinical education page; accessed 2026-08-16
source_locator: T4 Tests — interpretation of combined TSH and FT4/FTI results
source_claim_supported: Elevated TSH with low free T4/FTI indicates primary hypothyroidism; low TSH with low FT4 suggests pituitary-related hypothyroidism, and low TSH with elevated FT4 indicates hyperthyroidism.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
blueprint_locator: Printed p.13, Reduction of Risk Potential — review and interpret laboratory and diagnostic results
blueprint_topic: Reduction of Risk Potential — thyroid-function test interpretation

source_original.stem: A client's free T4 level is below the normal range, along with an elevated TSH, and a new nurse assumes these two abnormal values together must point toward an overactive thyroid. The nurse should recognize this specific combination as consistent with:

options.A: A laboratory pattern unrelated to thyroid function or pituitary regulation
options.B: Primary hypothyroidism with low free T4 and compensatory elevation of TSH
options.C: Normal thyroid function despite abnormal free T4 and TSH concentrations
options.D: Primary hyperthyroidism with excessive thyroid hormone and suppressed TSH

source_original.rationale: A low free T4 combined with an elevated TSH is the classic laboratory pattern of primary hypothyroidism, in which the thyroid gland is underproducing thyroid hormone, prompting increased pituitary TSH secretion in an attempt to stimulate more hormone production.
source_original.source_detail: Elevated TSH with low free T4 indicates primary hypothyroidism; current patient/clinical education page, accessed 2026-08-14.

correction_summary: Removed narrative cueing and explanatory options, converted choices to concise diagnostic patterns, verified the exact ATA TSH/FT4 interpretation, and reduced difficulty from hard to easy.

audit_findings.source_authority: American Thyroid Association; NCSBN 2026 Test Plan
audit_findings.currentness: ATA thyroid-function interpretation page remains current at 2026-08-16.
audit_findings.claim_audit: The exact elevated-TSH/low-FT4 combination is directly stated by ATA to indicate primary hypothyroidism.

distractor_audit.B: Primary hyperthyroidism has the opposite TSH/thyroid-hormone pattern.
distractor_audit.C: Central hypothyroidism does not typically produce appropriately elevated TSH.
distractor_audit.D: Both values are abnormal and do not represent euthyroid function.

audit_findings.ambiguity_second_answer: Assay interference and unusual pituitary TSH biology can complicate rare cases, but the stem asks the standard pattern; among listed choices A is uniquely best.
audit_findings.cueing: Final options are diagnosis labels of similar form; no explanatory phrase gives away the answer.
audit_findings.blueprint: Reduction of Risk Potential is appropriate for laboratory interpretation.
audit_findings.independent_second_pass: Re-read the ATA T4 Tests section and NCBI thyroid physiology comparison, challenged central hypothyroidism as a possible alternative, and confirmed A remained uniquely correct for the stated pattern.
